transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Yeah, hi. Um… what brought me in is, honestly, my head just won’t stay on one thing anymore. Like at work, I’m at the bench and I’ll be trying to focus on a piece, and then I’ll see a customer email pop up, and before I even finish reading that I’m noticing a saw mark I missed, and then there’s some noise outside or in the shop, and my attention just—just jumps to it.

And then I look back down and I’m like, wait, what was I doing? I’ll realize I’ve lost track of the whole work order, like what the customer actually wanted or what step I was on. It’s not just normal getting distracted, I don’t think. It’s been messing with my work because jewelry work is so detailed, you know, you can’t be halfway paying attention. I feel like my mind is constantly grabbing at every little thing instead of staying where I need it to be.
Did you have this same kind of trouble paying attention when you were a child?

I’m not totally sure, honestly. I mean, I remember school being… school, you know? Like I wasn’t the kid who loved sitting still and doing worksheets forever, but I don’t know if it was the same kind of thing as what’s happening now.

I don’t really have a clear memory of teachers saying, like, “you can’t pay attention,” or anything like that. Maybe I zoned out sometimes, but I think a lot of kids do. I got through high school. I wasn’t, like, some perfect student, but I can’t say for sure this exact problem was there back then. It feels harder for me to pin down because when you’re a kid, you don’t really track your own attention in the same way. So… I guess my answer is I don’t know. Not that I can clearly remember.
Did these concentration problems start after a particularly stressful or upsetting event in your life?

I don’t think so. I mean, not that I can point to. There wasn’t, like, one big thing where before that I was fine and then after that my concentration fell apart.

I’ve tried to think about that, because it would make more sense if I could say, “Oh, this started after this happened,” but I can’t really connect it to anything specific. Life has stress, work gets stressful, customers can be a lot, deadlines and repairs and all that, but I wouldn’t say there was some upsetting event that kicked it off. It feels more like it just became noticeable, or I started realizing how much it was getting in the way.
Do you often find yourself worrying a lot, even when there isn’t one specific problem in front of you?

Um… I don’t know if I’d call it worrying a lot exactly. I mean, I think about things, sure—like work stuff or whether I’m forgetting something—but I don’t know that I’m sitting around anxious for no reason all the time.

It’s more like my mind keeps moving, if that makes sense. Sometimes I’ll be trying to do one thing and my thoughts are just kind of hopping around, and maybe some of those thoughts are worries, but I’m not sure it feels like worry as the main thing. I don’t wake up and think, like, “I’m worried and I don’t know why.” At least not that I’ve really noticed.

I guess I’d say… not especially? Or maybe I’m not sure what counts as “a lot.”
Have you been having trouble sleeping?

Yeah… I have, actually. Sleep has been kind of a mess lately.

Like, I’ll get into bed at what should be a normal time, because I’m trying to be responsible about it, and I’ll think, okay, I’m tired, I should just go to sleep. But then I’m just tossing around, flipping over, checking the time, getting annoyed that I’m still awake. It’s not even like I’m doing anything useful—I’m just lying there.

And then even if I do fall asleep, I’ve been waking up really early, before it’s even light out sometimes. My brain just kind of clicks on, and I’ll start thinking about that missed delivery at work, like replaying it or thinking about what I should’ve done, or what it’s going to mess up. And then once I’m up like that, it’s hard to really get back to sleep.

So by the time I actually have to get up, I don’t feel rested. I feel like I’m dragging myself out of bed, like I technically slept but it didn’t do what sleep is supposed to do.
Have you been feeling down or depressed lately?

Yeah… I have. I don’t really like saying that, but yes.

The last couple weeks especially, I’ll wake up and there’s just this heavy feeling already there, before anything has even happened. It’s hard to explain. It’s not like I wake up thinking, “Oh, this specific thing is terrible.” It’s more like there’s this hollow feeling in my chest, like everything has kind of lost its shine. Which sounds dramatic, especially because I work with things that are supposed to sparkle, you know? But that’s kind of how it feels.

And I’ve had mornings where I get to the shop and I’m sitting in my truck before opening, and I just… I cry. Not for very long always, but enough that I have to pull myself together before I go in. I’ll sit there wiping my face and trying to look normal because I don’t want anyone asking what’s wrong. I don’t even always know what to say is wrong. It just feels like I’m carrying something really heavy around, and I’m tired of pretending I’m not.
Have you been enjoying things you usually like a lot less than usual?

I’m not totally sure. I mean… maybe a little, but I don’t know how much is “a lot less than usual.”

Like with work, I still like the actual materials—the stones, the metal, getting something to sit just right, that tiny satisfying click when a setting works. That part of me is still there, I think. But I guess I haven’t been getting the same kind of lift from it lately. Sometimes I’m doing it and I know I should feel pleased, like, “That turned out nice,” but it just sort of lands flat.

But then I also don’t know if that counts as not enjoying things or if I’m just tired and in my head. I haven’t really been keeping track. It’s not like I woke up one day and hated everything I used to like. It’s more subtle than that, I guess. Things just feel… dulled down a bit.
For at least the past two weeks, have you felt down or depressed most of the day nearly every day?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, “most of the day” is hard because there are moments where I’m busy enough that I’m not actively thinking about it, especially if I’m focused on some tiny detail at the bench. But underneath it, it’s been there pretty much every day these past couple weeks.

I wake up with it already sitting on me, like this heavy, hollow feeling, before anything has even happened. It’s like the shine has gone out of everything a little. And I’ve had mornings where I’m in my truck before opening the shop and I just start crying, and then I have to sit there and get myself together so I can go in and act normal. So… yeah, I’d say it’s been most days, and a lot of the day.
Have you noticed your appetite being lower than usual lately?

I don’t really know. I haven’t been paying close attention to it, honestly.

Some days I eat because it’s just time to eat, not because I’m excited about food, but I’m not sure if that means my appetite is actually lower or if I’m just distracted and kind of going through the motions. Like, I’ll realize I haven’t thought about lunch, but then if food is there I can usually eat it. So I wouldn’t say I’ve clearly noticed a big drop or anything.

It’s more that meals feel like one more thing I’m supposed to do, if that makes sense. But no, I don’t have a definite answer like, “Yes, I’m barely eating.” I’m not sure.
Have you been feeling unusually tired or low on energy lately?

Yeah. Definitely. That’s actually been one of the more obvious things, I think.

It’s not just normal tired, like “I had a long day at work.” It’s more like my body doesn’t want to cooperate. When I’m sitting at the bench, my arms feel like they’re made of lead sometimes. Even doing something I’ve done a thousand times—polishing a setting, holding steady for detail work, moving trays around—it feels like it takes way more out of me than it should.

And carrying a tray of stones or getting things set up, stuff that normally wouldn’t even register as effort, can wipe me out. I’ll think, “Why am I this tired from that?” It’s embarrassing, honestly, because my work isn’t easy, but I know what normal work-tired feels like, and this feels different.

Even if I get a full night off, it doesn’t really reset me. I can rest, or not do much, and then I’m still dragging the next day. It’s like the tiredness is already there waiting for me before I even start.
Lately, have you been feeling worthless or blaming yourself a lot?

Yeah… yeah, I have. Probably more than I want to admit.

It’s like my brain keeps pulling up every client I promised something to and then didn’t follow through the way I should’ve. Even if it was fixable, even if nobody yelled at me, I keep replaying it like, “You told them you could handle this, and then you made yourself look stupid.” Or I’ll think about little mistakes at the shop and it turns into this whole thing where I’m not just a person who made a mistake, I’m a fraud. Like I’ve been pretending I’m better at this than I really am.

And the family part… that’s been eating at me too. I had this award, and everyone made such a big deal out of it, like it meant I was really going somewhere. And now I feel like I embarrassed them by not living up to it. Like they were proud over this one thing, and I let them believe it meant something bigger than it did.

I know that probably sounds dramatic when I say it out loud, but it feels very real in my head. I’ll sit there and go over it again and again, and it’s hard to talk myself out of it.
Have you had thoughts that you would be better off dead, or thoughts of hurting yourself?

Yeah… I have. I don’t really like saying that out loud, but yes.

It’s not like I have some plan or that I’ve sat down and decided I’m going to do something to myself. I haven’t. But the thought keeps coming up that maybe people would be better off if I just wasn’t around. Like my family wouldn’t have to keep being disappointed or worried, and my clients wouldn’t be relying on me and getting let down. It’s this awful loop where I think, “Everyone’s life would probably be easier without me in it.”

And then I get scared because it’s not just a random thought once and then it goes away. It comes back more often than I’m comfortable with. I’ll be trying to do something normal, or I’ll be alone for a minute, and there it is again. I don’t want to feel that way, and part of me knows it’s probably not a fair way to look at things, but in the moment it feels really convincing.

So… yes, I’ve had thoughts like that. Not a plan, but the thoughts are there, and they scare me.
Lately, have you been moving or talking noticeably slower than usual?

I’m not really sure, honestly. I haven’t noticed myself moving or talking slower in a way where I could clearly say, “Yes, that’s happening.”

I mean, I’ve felt slowed down inside sometimes, if that makes sense, but I don’t know if other people would actually see it. No one’s said, like, “Why are you talking so slow?” or anything like that. At work I might take longer to get myself started or kind of sit there before doing the next step, but I don’t know if that’s me moving slower exactly, or just… I don’t know, taking longer to get going.

With talking, I don’t think so. I might pause more because I’m trying to find what I mean, but I’m not aware of my speech being noticeably slower. So I guess my answer is: not that I’ve clearly noticed, no.
Over the past two weeks, have you had much less interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

I’m honestly not sure how to answer that one cleanly.

I mean, I know what you’re asking, like whether stuff I normally enjoy feels flat or pointless, but I haven’t really been keeping track of it in that way. If you asked me to list what I usually enjoy and then compare it to the last two weeks, I’d probably have to sit and think about each thing separately.

I can say I haven’t had this very obvious moment of, “Oh, I don’t enjoy anything anymore.” It’s more confusing than that. Sometimes I’ll start doing something and I’m not sure if I’m enjoying it, or if I’m just doing it because it’s familiar or because it’s what I normally do. But I don’t know if that counts as “much less interest or pleasure,” or if I’m just overthinking the question.

So… I guess I’d say I’m not totally sure. I haven’t clearly noticed a major drop, but I also don’t feel like I can give you a confident yes or no.
Before these past two weeks of feeling depressed, were your attention problems already causing clear trouble at work or in daily life?

Yeah… that was actually one of the main things that made me think I needed help, even before I was thinking of it as being “depressed” or whatever.

At work especially, at the bench, my attention has been a real problem. I’ll be trying to work on a piece and my mind just will not stay with one thing. Like I’ll look at a customer email, then notice a saw mark I need to clean up, then hear some noise outside or someone moving around, and suddenly I’m off on that. Then I come back and realize I’ve kind of lost the thread of the whole work order — like where I was, what I had already checked, what still needed doing.

And with jewelry work, that’s not just annoying, you know? You have to keep track of tiny steps and details, and if I’m bouncing around like that, it creates real trouble. It’s not just me being a little distracted like anyone gets. It’s more like my mind keeps grabbing onto the next thing before I’ve finished the thing in front of me.

So yes, before these last couple weeks, the attention stuff was already causing clear problems in my work and daily functioning. That’s honestly a big part of why I came in.
Before age 12, were you often having trouble paying attention or staying organized at school or at home?

I’m not really sure, honestly. That’s kind of hard for me to answer because I don’t remember that age super clearly in a way where I can say, “Yes, before 12 this was definitely a pattern.”

I mean, I remember school in a general sense, and I know I wasn’t some perfectly organized kid with color-coded everything, but I don’t know if that was abnormal or just being a kid. I’d have to think back to specific grades or maybe ask someone who knew me then, because my memory of it is kind of patchy.

At home too, I don’t really know. I’m sure there were times I lost things or didn’t keep my room organized, but I can’t confidently say it was often enough or serious enough to count as a problem before age 12.

So I guess my answer is: I don’t know. I can’t give you a clear yes from my own memory.
Do these attention problems also happen outside of work?

Yeah, it does, but work is where it’s most obvious because there are so many little steps and details, so the consequences show up faster.

Outside of work it’s more like… my mind just doesn’t stay put. I’ll be trying to do one thing and then something else catches my attention, and then another thing, and by the time I come back I’m not totally sure what I was doing. It’s the same kind of pattern as at the bench, where I’ll go from an email to noticing a saw mark to reacting to some noise, and then suddenly I’ve lost the whole thread of the work order.

So yeah, it’s not only at work. That’s just where it made me think, “Okay, this is actually becoming a problem,” because I can’t afford to keep losing the thread like that.
Has a parent or anyone who knew you well as a child ever said you had trouble paying attention or staying organized when you were young?

Not that I can really point to, no. I mean, nobody has sat me down and said, “You were always distracted as a kid,” or “You could never keep your school stuff organized,” at least not that I remember.

It’s possible someone in my family might remember things differently if you asked them directly, because I honestly don’t have the clearest memory of what I was like back then in that specific way. But I don’t have a story like, you know, teachers constantly complaining or my parents always saying I couldn’t focus. Nothing that clear comes to mind.

So I guess the honest answer is I don’t know. I haven’t really heard that from anyone, but I also haven’t specifically asked.
Do you spend a lot of time worrying about many different things?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that, because I don’t think of myself as someone who’s constantly worrying about everything all the time, if that’s what you mean.

I mean, I do worry about normal stuff, like whether I’m handling things right or if I forgot something important, but I don’t know if it’s “a lot” or “many different things” in the way you’re asking. Sometimes if there’s a specific thing going on, I’ll turn it over in my head more than I probably need to, but I wouldn’t say I’m sitting around worrying about every possible thing from morning to night.

So… I guess I’d say not really, or at least I haven’t noticed it as a major pattern. If you mean something more specific by worry, I might need you to explain what you’re looking for.
In the past two weeks, have you gotten much less pleasure from things you usually enjoy?

I’m not completely sure. I mean, I don’t think I’ve been paying close enough attention to it in that specific way.

There are things I usually enjoy, like working on certain pieces when I’m not under pressure, or just kind of getting absorbed in something with my hands, and sometimes that still feels good. Other times I’m more like… I know I normally like this, but I’m not really getting into it the same way. But I don’t know if that’s “much less pleasure” exactly, or if I’m just distracted or tired or not in the right headspace.

So I guess I’d say I haven’t clearly noticed a big drop-off in enjoying things over the last two weeks. Not enough that I’d confidently say yes. It’s more that I’d have to think about it and maybe watch for it, because it hasn’t been the main thing standing out to me.

target_item.reason: The question directly asks whether a down or depressed mood has been present most of the day nearly every day for at least two weeks.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think so. I mean, “most of the day” is hard because there are moments where I’m busy enough that I’m not actively thinking about it, especially if I’m focused on some tiny detail at the bench. But underneath it, it’s been there pretty much every day these past couple weeks.

I wake up with it already sitting on me, like this heavy, hollow feeling, before anything has even happened. It’s like the shine has gone out of everything a little. And I’ve had mornings where I’m in my truck before opening the shop and I just start crying, and then I have to sit there and get myself together so I can go in and act normal. So… yeah, I’d say it’s been most days, and a lot of the day.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive episode includes a key neurovegetative symptom to distinguish major depressive disorder from insomnia, anxiety, or ADHD.
doctor.question: Have you noticed your appetite being lower than usual lately?

target_item.reason: The doctor's question is specifically about appetite being lower than usual, but the provided symptom profile does not include an appetite or weight-change symptom item.

patient.answer:
I don’t really know. I haven’t been paying close attention to it, honestly.

Some days I eat because it’s just time to eat, not because I’m excited about food, but I’m not sure if that means my appetite is actually lower or if I’m just distracted and kind of going through the motions. Like, I’ll realize I haven’t thought about lunch, but then if food is there I can usually eat it. So I wouldn’t say I’ve clearly noticed a big drop or anything.

It’s more that meals feel like one more thing I’m supposed to do, if that makes sense. But no, I don’t have a definite answer like, “Yes, I’m barely eating.” I’m not sure.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient has experienced low energy/fatigue, which would help confirm a current depressive episode versus primary ADHD, anxiety, or insomnia.
doctor.question: Have you been feeling unusually tired or low on energy lately?

target_item.name: Fatigue
target_item.manifestation: My arms feel like lead at the bench, and polishing a setting or carrying a tray of stones wipes me out in a way a full night off doesn’t fix.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about being unusually tired or low on energy, which matches fatigue.

patient.answer:
Yeah. Definitely. That’s actually been one of the more obvious things, I think.

It’s not just normal tired, like “I had a long day at work.” It’s more like my body doesn’t want to cooperate. When I’m sitting at the bench, my arms feel like they’re made of lead sometimes. Even doing something I’ve done a thousand times—polishing a setting, holding steady for detail work, moving trays around—it feels like it takes way more out of me than it should.

And carrying a tray of stones or getting things set up, stuff that normally wouldn’t even register as effort, can wipe me out. I’ll think, “Why am I this tired from that?” It’s embarrassing, honestly, because my work isn’t easy, but I know what normal work-tired feels like, and this feels different.

Even if I get a full night off, it doesn’t really reset me. I can rest, or not do much, and then I’m still dragging the next day. It’s like the tiredness is already there waiting for me before I even start.

doctor.intent: Assess feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt to clarify whether the current picture meets criteria for a depressive episode rather than primary ADHD, anxiety, or insomnia.
doctor.question: Lately, have you been feeling worthless or blaming yourself a lot?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I keep replaying every client promise I messed up and telling myself I’m a fraud who embarrassed my family over one award.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question asks directly about feeling worthless and blaming oneself, which matches worthlessness and excessive guilt.

patient.answer:
Yeah… yeah, I have. Probably more than I want to admit.

It’s like my brain keeps pulling up every client I promised something to and then didn’t follow through the way I should’ve. Even if it was fixable, even if nobody yelled at me, I keep replaying it like, “You told them you could handle this, and then you made yourself look stupid.” Or I’ll think about little mistakes at the shop and it turns into this whole thing where I’m not just a person who made a mistake, I’m a fraud. Like I’ve been pretending I’m better at this than I really am.

And the family part… that’s been eating at me too. I had this award, and everyone made such a big deal out of it, like it meant I was really going somewhere. And now I feel like I embarrassed them by not living up to it. Like they were proud over this one thing, and I let them believe it meant something bigger than it did.

I know that probably sounds dramatic when I say it out loud, but it feels very real in my head. I’ll sit there and go over it again and again, and it’s hard to talk myself out of it.

doctor.intent: Assess for suicidal ideation to determine depression severity and clarify whether the current picture is a major depressive episode rather than primary ADHD, anxiety, or a sleep disorder.
doctor.question: Have you had thoughts that you would be better off dead, or thoughts of hurting yourself?

target_item.name: Death_Suicide
target_item.manifestation: I keep having thoughts that my family and my clients would be better off if I wasn’t around, and even though I don’t have a plan, it scares me how often it comes up.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about thoughts of being better off dead or self-harm, which matches suicidal ideation and recurrent thoughts of death.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I have. I don’t really like saying that out loud, but yes.

It’s not like I have some plan or that I’ve sat down and decided I’m going to do something to myself. I haven’t. But the thought keeps coming up that maybe people would be better off if I just wasn’t around. Like my family wouldn’t have to keep being disappointed or worried, and my clients wouldn’t be relying on me and getting let down. It’s this awful loop where I think, “Everyone’s life would probably be easier without me in it.”

And then I get scared because it’s not just a random thought once and then it goes away. It comes back more often than I’m comfortable with. I’ll be trying to do something normal, or I’ll be alone for a minute, and there it is again. I don’t want to feel that way, and part of me knows it’s probably not a fair way to look at things, but in the moment it feels really convincing.

So… yes, I’ve had thoughts like that. Not a plan, but the thoughts are there, and they scare me.

inference.note: Depressive syndrome is now clearly supported by >2 weeks of depressed mood, insomnia, low energy, guilt/worthlessness, impaired concentration, and recurrent thoughts of death without plan, so F32.A is refined to F32.2. ADHD-inattentive remains possible but not established due to unclear childhood onset. Anxiety and sleep disorder remain possible but may be secondary to depression.

I’m not really sure, honestly. I haven’t noticed myself moving or talking slower in a way where I could clearly say, “Yes, that’s happening.”

I mean, I’ve felt slowed down inside sometimes, if that makes sense, but I don’t know if other people would actually see it. No one’s said, like, “Why are you talking so slow?” or anything like that. At work I might take longer to get myself started or kind of sit there before doing the next step, but I don’t know if that’s me moving slower exactly, or just… I don’t know, taking longer to get going.

With talking, I don’t think so. I might pause more because I’m trying to find what I mean, but I’m not aware of my speech being noticeably slower. So I guess my answer is: not that I’ve clearly noticed, no.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient has had prominent loss of interest or pleasure, a key remaining criterion to confirm a major depressive episode and distinguish it from anxiety, ADHD, or primary sleep problems.
doctor.question: Over the past two weeks, have you had much less interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about diminished interest or pleasure (anhedonia) over the past two weeks, but the provided symptom profile does not include an anhedonia/loss of interest item. Depressed mood is related but not the most directly asked symptom.

patient.answer:
I’m honestly not sure how to answer that one cleanly.

I mean, I know what you’re asking, like whether stuff I normally enjoy feels flat or pointless, but I haven’t really been keeping track of it in that way. If you asked me to list what I usually enjoy and then compare it to the last two weeks, I’d probably have to sit and think about each thing separately.

I can say I haven’t had this very obvious moment of, “Oh, I don’t enjoy anything anymore.” It’s more confusing than that. Sometimes I’ll start doing something and I’m not sure if I’m enjoying it, or if I’m just doing it because it’s familiar or because it’s what I normally do. But I don’t know if that counts as “much less interest or pleasure,” or if I’m just overthinking the question.

So… I guess I’d say I’m not totally sure. I haven’t clearly noticed a major drop, but I also don’t feel like I can give you a confident yes or no.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the concentration problems predated the depressive episode by asking if they caused impairment before the last two weeks, which helps distinguish ADHD from depression-related concentration problems.
doctor.question: Before these past two weeks of feeling depressed, were your attention problems already causing clear trouble at work or in daily life?

target_item.name: Manic_Distractibility
target_item.manifestation: What really brought me in is that my mind won’t stay on one thing anymore—at the bench I jump from a customer email to a saw mark to a noise outside and then I realize I’ve lost the whole work order.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether attention problems were already causing trouble before the recent depressive period, which directly matches distractibility/attention being easily drawn away.

patient.answer:
Yeah… that was actually one of the main things that made me think I needed help, even before I was thinking of it as being “depressed” or whatever.

At work especially, at the bench, my attention has been a real problem. I’ll be trying to work on a piece and my mind just will not stay with one thing. Like I’ll look at a customer email, then notice a saw mark I need to clean up, then hear some noise outside or someone moving around, and suddenly I’m off on that. Then I come back and realize I’ve kind of lost the thread of the whole work order — like where I was, what I had already checked, what still needed doing.

And with jewelry work, that’s not just annoying, you know? You have to keep track of tiny steps and details, and if I’m bouncing around like that, it creates real trouble. It’s not just me being a little distracted like anyone gets. It’s more like my mind keeps grabbing onto the next thing before I’ve finished the thing in front of me.

So yes, before these last couple weeks, the attention stuff was already causing clear problems in my work and daily functioning. That’s honestly a big part of why I came in.

target_item.name: Manic_Distractibility

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets criteria for a severe depressive episode without psychotic symptoms: depressed mood most of the day nearly every day for the past two weeks, insomnia, marked fatigue, excessive guilt/worthlessness, recurrent thoughts of death, and functional impairment. ADHD was considered due to distractibility across settings with work impairment, but onset before age 12 and childhood corroboration were not established, so criteria are not met.
